extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of literary fiction; aspiring authors interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Advice embedded in a literary narrative about how to construct and present a story: where to begin and end, what to include or omit, how to signal choices at branching points, how to define key terms, and how to place anecdotes and digressions for best effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative selection and emphasis (what to put in / leave out)
rubrics_metrics.description: "show him, where he is to begin it—and where he is to end it—what he is to put into it—and what he is to leave out—how much of it he is to cast into a shade—and whereabouts he is to throw his light!"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The storyteller should deliberately choose the material to include or omit and consciously decide degrees of emphasis (what to highlight and what to shade). These choices determine whether the tale is 'worth the hearing' and shape readers' attention and emotional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear signaling at narrative junctions / transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: "wherever in any part of your dominions it so falls out, that three several roads meet in one point... that at least you set up a guide-post in the centre of them, in mere charity, to direct an uncertain devil which of the three he is to take."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple threads, episodes, or possible directions converge, provide clear signals (like a 'guide-post') so the reader knows which path the narrative will follow. This prevents confusion when the story could legitimately proceed in several different ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of anecdotes and digressions (avoid premature anticipation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator worries that an anecdote 'in one sense, is certainly out of its place here; for by right it should come in... but then if I reserve it for either of those parts of my story—I ruin the story I'm upon;—and if I tell it here—I anticipate matters, and ruin it there.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes and digressions must be sited with regard to narrative economy: placing them in the wrong spot can spoil the current thread or pre-empt later developments. Weigh the costs of interrupting the present narrative against the costs of delaying the anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define key terms precisely before use
rubrics_metrics.description: "In books of strict morality and close reasoning... what have you to do, before you set out... unless you intend to go puzzling on to the day of judgment—but to give the world a good definition..." and the long example: defining 'Nose' with 'all possible exactness and precision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before relying on a particular term or conceit throughout a piece (especially in argumentative or moralizing passages), give a clear, fixed definition so readers aren't misled. This reduces equivocation and prevents later misunderstandings or spurious objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphors with caution in factual or historical narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Parenthetical admonition: 'to drop my metaphor (for there is nothing more dishonest in an historian than the use of one)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contexts that claim factuality or close reasoning (e.g., history, moral argument), metaphors can mislead or appear dishonest. Prefer literal clarity in such passages; reserve metaphoric flourish for clearly fictional or rhetorical moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support unusual claims with research or authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The father 'collected every book and treatise which had been systematically wrote upon noses' to back up his odd opinion about long noses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making idiosyncratic or surprising assertions, bolster them with references, examples, or documented sources. As demonstrated by the character's collection of treatises, assembling authorities strengthens an eccentric claim and helps defend it against critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to tell a story 'worth the hearing' (engagement as a criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator invokes the 'powers... which enable mortal man to tell a story worth the hearing' — powers that 'kindly shew him, where he is to begin it—and where he is to end it...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical choices, the ultimate evaluative standard for narrative is whether it is compelling and well-told. Structural decisions (beginning/end, inclusion/exclusion, emphasis) should serve the higher aim of producing an engaging, meaningful story.
